extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer offices, research administrators, university legal counsel, small business and nonprofit contractors receiving federal funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal requirements for nonprofit organizations and small businesses to retain title to inventions arising from federally funded research, including disclosure, election, filing, licensing, and consequences of noncompliance under the Bayh-Dole Act and implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on third-party participation in inter partes reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIPA, on patents issuing from applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, a third party requesting reexamination can participate to a limited extent in the reexamination process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific limitations include: the third-party requestor can file one written comment on each PTO action and applicant response; the third-party requestor can appeal to the Board of Appeals of the PTO but not to the federal circuit court; the patent owner may appeal a final rejection of claims to the Board of Appeals of the PTO or to the federal court of appeals and can seek a stay of any pending litigation involving any claim subject to inter partes reexamination. Also, a third-party requestor is estopped from later (e.g., in litigation) raising issues they 'raised or could have raised' in the reexamination, and any requestor is estopped from later challenging 'any fact' determined in the reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-user rights defense (AIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIPA creates a defense to patent infringement for certain prior users for lawsuits filed after November 29, 1999.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense is limited to methods of doing or conducting business (e.g., financial and e-commerce patents). The infringing party must have practiced the method at least one year before the patentee filed its application and commercially exploited the method before the patentee filed its patent application. Assertion of the prior-use defense does not render the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely disclosure of subject inventions (two-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The small business or nonprofit organization must disclose each subject invention to the funding agency within two months after the inventor discloses it in writing to the entity’s personnel responsible for patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be a written report identifying the inventors and the contract under which the invention was made, and must be sufficiently complete in technical detail to convey a clear understanding of the invention (nature, purpose, operation, characteristics) and must identify any publication, sale, or public use. After disclosure the entity must promptly notify the agency of acceptance of any manuscript or of any planned sale or public use. Requests for extension may be granted at the agency's discretion. Use of iEdison is recommended to manage reporting; audits compare institutional records with agency and PTO records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election to retain title (two-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The small business or nonprofit organization must submit a written election to retain title prior to the earlier of two years from the date of disclosure of the subject invention to the funding agency or the occurrence of a statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency may shorten the election period if a one-year statutory period has been initiated by publication, sale, or public use (but not to more than 60 days prior to the end of the statutory period). Requests for extension may be granted at agency discretion. If the organization fails to elect timely, the funding agency may request title be conveyed to it (request must be in writing and submitted within 60 days of the agency learning of the failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and requirements for filing patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization must file its initial patent application on subject inventions it elects to retain within specified timeframes to avoid statutory bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File the initial U.S. application within one year after election of title or, if earlier, prior to the end of any statutory period for valid U.S. patent protection after publication, sale, or public use. File foreign applications within ten months of the corresponding initial patent application or within six months after permission is granted following a secrecy order. Funding agencies may grant extensions. All patent applications and issued patents must include a statement that the invention was made with government support and that the U.S. government has certain rights (example citation provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of U.S. government license
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bayh-Dole Act requires automatic granting to the U.S. government of a license when an organization elects to retain title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government receives a nonexclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license to practice or have practiced on its behalf throughout the world any subject invention to which title is retained. This allows government researchers and contractors to use or produce the invention for government purposes. Third parties (contractors, grantees) can use the government's licenses as permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote utilization, commercialization, and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations electing to retain title must promote the invention’s utilization, commercialization, and public availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a continuing obligation under Bayh-Dole and a factor considered by funding agencies; failure to promote may implicate agency actions such as march-in rights or other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall not assign the invention except under limited conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment is permitted only to an organization which has as one of its primary functions the management of inventions, and any assignee must be subject to the same provisions as the contractor (i.e., the same Bayh-Dole obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty distribution and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must share royalty income with inventors and use remaining royalty income appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalties must be shared with inventors, and remaining royalty income should be used for research and education as required by Bayh-Dole implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference to small businesses and U.S. industry
rubrics_metrics.description: When commercializing subject inventions, organizations must provide certain preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a preference to small businesses and provide a preference to U.S. industry as part of obligations to promote commercialization and public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to comply with Bayh-Dole obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet reporting, election, filing, or other obligations may trigger agency remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The funding agency may take title to the invention or exercise march-in rights under 35 U.S.C. § 203; the agency may also discontinue providing federal research funds. Example: Campbell Plastics case where improper disclosure led to forfeiture of title. Agencies may request title be conveyed within sixty days of learning of a failure to disclose or elect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where agency may require title transfer to U.S. government
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bayh-Dole Act does not apply universally; agencies may require government ownership in specified situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations include: the awardee is not located in the U.S. or is under foreign government control; the agency determines an exceptional circumstance exists; a federal foreign intelligence/counterintelligence authority requires restriction for security; agreements involving certain DOE contractor-operated facilities dedicated to naval nuclear-propulsion or weapons-related programs; and funding agreements with the Tennessee Valley Authority. Conversely, agencies may not require rights in awards made primarily for educational purposes (scholarships, fellowships, training grants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'subject invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject invention is any invention conceived or first actually reduced to practice in the performance of work under a funding agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject inventions need not be fully funded by federal support or fall within the statement of work; the key is conception or first actual reduction to practice in performance of the funded work. Determinations may involve factual analysis and agency/regulatory interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling overlapping government and non-government-funded research
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules to determine whether inventions arising in mixed-funded environments are subject to Bayh-Dole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a closely related non-government-funded project falls outside the scope of the planned and committed activities of the federally funded project and does not diminish or distract from performance of those activities, inventions made in the non-government-funded project are not subject to Bayh-Dole. Time relationship between projects is not a dispositive factor. Because it is difficult to prove independence, many institutions adopt co-mingling policies deeming inventions from labs with federal funds to be subject inventions unless proven otherwise, requiring written evidence to show independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for written assignment agreements from researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: To retain title, institutions must ensure inventors assign rights appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should require by written agreement (employment agreements, research contracts, fund-disbursement agreements) that employees, students, and collaborators disclose inventions and assign rights to the institution. Students and other non-employees are often not automatically bound, so institutions should obtain explicit assignment or at least research-use/license rights to avoid losing title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure content and post-disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: What must be included in the disclosure and what subsequent notifications are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures must identify inventors and contract, give sufficient technical detail (nature, purpose, operation, characteristics), and identify prior or planned publication, sale, or public use; the entity must promptly notify the agency if a manuscript is accepted or if a sale/public use is planned. Requests for extension of disclosure deadlines may be granted at agency discretion. Institutions should document actions and be prepared for audits comparing institutional disclosures with agency and PTO records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency remedies and organization license if title conveyed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency requests and obtains title, certain licenses and limitations apply to the original organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If title is conveyed to the funding agency, the organization will retain a nonexclusive, royalty-free license throughout the world to that subject invention; the license extends to domestic subsidiaries and affiliates and may be transferred only with agency approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor election and organization rights when organization declines title
rubrics_metrics.description: If the organization declines to retain title, the right to elect title passes to the funding agency which may allow the inventor to retain title under conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the funding agency does not elect title, the inventor may petition to retain title. If the agency grants the inventor title, the inventor remains obligated to protect U.S. government interests (file patents, provide preferences to U.S. industry and small businesses). The organization may not have license rights if the inventor obtains title, so institutions should consider policies requiring inventors who retain title to grant at least research rights back to the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify agency before discontinuing prosecution or maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must inform the funding agency if they decide not to continue patent prosecution, pay maintenance fees, or defend in reexamination/opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written notice of such a determination must be provided to the funding agency within thirty days before the expiration of the response period required by the relevant patent office. The funding agency may then take title in those countries where the organization fails to file timely or decides not to continue prosecution or maintenance; if title is conveyed, the organization retains a nonexclusive, royalty-free license as noted above.
